MESA Core architecture enforces rigid four-level scope metadata on every memory query. Retrieval routers filter by `(tenant_id, workspace_id, agent_id)` at the database engine level before any vector or graph computation takes place.

en.title: Dense embeddings vs sparse lexical representations in search
en.subtitle: Understanding continuous geometric spaces and discrete inverted token indexes
en.summary: Dense embeddings excel at conceptual meaning across vocabulary gaps, while sparse representations capture exact term matches and rare identifiers.
en.shortAnswer: Dense models map meaning into dense float vectors; sparse models map exact tokens into high-dimensional keyword weights. Hybrid pipelines require both.

sections.title: The vocabulary mismatch vs exact identifier paradox

blocks.text: Dense vectors compress texts into 768 or 1536 floating point numbers. This compression bridges synonyms but erases exact character sequences, making dense models unreliable for finding unique docket numbers or software error codes.

blocks.title: The Exact Identifier Failure Mode
blocks.text: Querying a dense index for 'Article 314/2' often returns 'Article 314/1' or 'Article 312' with 0.94 cosine similarity, because the dense model represents the legal topic rather than the discrete statutory sub-clause.

rows: High: captures paraphrases and conceptual affinity
Low: strictly dependent on token frequency and co-occurrence
Low: rare tokens suffer from tokenization compression
Extremely high: rare words receive highest IDF weights
Compact: inverted lists compressed on disk
Robust: BM25 operates effectively on unseen vocabularies

sections.title: Continuous cosine distance vs BM25 term saturation

blocks.text: Dense search computes cosine similarity between continuous vectors: cos(u, v) = (u . v) / (||u|| ||v||). Sparse search uses BM25 probabilistic relevance: scoring documents based on term frequency (TF) and inverse document frequency (IDF) with length normalization.

blocks.code:
// Sparse BM25 Score calculation structure
Score(D, Q) = Σ IDF(q_i) * [ (f(q_i, D) * (k1 + 1)) / (f(q_i, D) + k1 * (1 - b + b * (|D| / avgdl))) ]

sections.title: MESA's dual vector and lexical lanes

blocks.text: MESA Core does not compromise between dense and sparse. It executes LanceDB dense vector search and SQLite FTS5 BM25 lexical search in parallel, fusing both ranked candidate lists using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

items: Dense vectors retrieve conceptual paraphrases and multilingual matches.
BM25 catches exact law article numbers, party names, and error codes.
Rank fusion eliminates the need to normalize incompatible raw scores.
Pre-filtering restricts both lanes to the authorized tenant partition.

en.summary: First-stage retrieval rapidly gathers candidate passages, while second-stage cross-encoder rerankers perform deep query-document cross-attention to eliminate false positives.

blocks.text: First-stage retrievers (bi-encoders and BM25) process queries and documents independently. Because query tokens cannot attend to document tokens during indexing, bi-encoders miss subtle logical relationships such as negation or conditional statements.

blocks.title: The Top-K Pollution Risk
blocks.text: Feeding unranked top-20 candidates directly into an agent's context window consumes precious token budget and injects distractors that confuse model reasoning.

rows: Dot product / Cosine distance between pre-computed vectors

Schema filter, evidence verification, temporal validity check

blocks.text: In a cross-encoder, the query and document are concatenated into a single sequence: `[CLS] Query [SEP] Document [SEP]`. Every transformer layer allows every query token to attend directly to every document token, capturing nuanced nuances like 'except', 'unless', and 'not'.

In MESA Core, hybrid first-stage retrieval surfaces candidates from vector, BM25, and graph lanes. Candidates are fused via RRF, reranked for precision, and passed through deterministic profile gates before prompt injection.

items: First-stage gathers broad candidate recall across complementary lanes.
Cross-encoder reranking eliminates lexical distractors and semantic near-misses.
Reranked results retain immutable pointers to canonical evidence spans.
Strict latency budgets ensure reranking does not breach interactive SLAs.

en.summary: Autonomous agents operating in regulated industries require immutable audit trails that record every prompt, memory retrieval, model output, and database mutation.

blocks.text: When an AI system commits a financial transaction or issues legal advice, standard application logs merely record that an HTTP request completed. blocks.title: The Tamper Vulnerability
blocks.text: Traditional database log tables can be modified or deleted by rogue administrators or compromised processes. Compliance audits in regulated domains mandate mathematically verifiable tamper-evidence.

sections.title: Cryptographic hash chaining in audit ledgers

blocks.text: Every audit event record contains a cryptographic hash of its payload combined with the hash of the preceding record: `H_i = SHA-256(Record_i || H_{i-1})`. Any retroactive modification to a historical event invalidates all downstream hash links.

MESA Core records every retrieval cycle and assertion lifecycle change in its canonical audit schema. Profile B security certification verifies that audit logs are tamper-evident and fail closed under unauthorized mutation attempts.

sections.title: Character offset anchoring and verification mathematics

blocks.text: An evidence span record anchors a factual proposition to an exact byte interval: `doc_sha256:span[c_start, c_end]`. During an audit, an automated checker fetches the original document by its hash, slices the bytes at `[c_start..c_end]`, and verifies that the text matches the recorded evidence quote.

In MESA Data and Core, raw official legal texts are preserved as immutable byte bedrock. Every assertion in SQLite maps to a verified evidence span. Frontends highlight the exact authoritative text in the official gazette when users inspect a claim.

items: Source documents are indexed by SHA-256 content hashes.

en.summary: Eliminating hallucinations requires a dual-stage architecture: restricting model generation strictly to retrieved evidence spans and verifying natural language entailment before delivery.
en.shortAnswer: Hallucination mitigation enforces strict grounding constraints: models must cite verifiable evidence spans and pass automated entailment checks.

blocks.text: Large language models are probabilistic text generators trained to predict plausible next tokens. In the absence of strict grounding boundaries, they fill factual gaps by generating statistically plausible fiction with high synthetic confidence.

blocks.title: The Fluent Hallucination Danger
blocks.text: The most dangerous hallucinations are not bizarre gibberish, but highly articulate, well-structured assertions that sound completely authoritative while being factually untrue.

rows: Negative constraints ('Answer only using facts below')
Moderate: models still leak parametric priors
Strict context injection of verified assertions only
Model must output explicit assertion keys for claims
Very High: binds statements to IDs

Highest: blocks ungrounded output before user delivery

blocks.text: Before a generated response is displayed to the user, an independent verification worker breaks the response into atomic propositions and runs an NLI classifier: `NLI(Evidence_Span, Generated_Proposition) -> {ENTAILMENT, NEUTRAL, CONTRADICTION}`. If any proposition scores NEUTRAL or CONTRADICTION, the response is rejected or flagged.

blocks.code:
// Automated entailment verification check
For each sentence in Model_Response:
    Proposition = ExtractClaim(sentence)
    Evidence = FetchCanonicalSpan(Proposition.citation_id)
    Score = NLI_Model.predict(premise=Evidence, hypothesis=Proposition)
    Assert Score.entailment > 0.90, 'Ungrounded claim detected!'

blocks.text: MESA adheres to a zero-trust grounding paradigm. The system never relies on an LLM's self-reported accuracy. Every response is generated from canonical SQLite assertions and verified against immutable evidence spans.

items: Prompt context contains only verified, scope-validated assertions.

Unverified claims fail closed and trigger explicit user notifications.

en.summary: Standard BM25 defaults (k1=1.2, b=0.75) are calibrated for general web documents. Highly structured legal statutes and code repositories require tailored parameters.
en.shortAnswer: Tuning k1 controls how fast multiple occurrences saturate relevance; tuning b controls how heavily long documents are penalized.

blocks.text: Information retrieval libraries commonly ship with hardcoded BM25 defaults calibrated on 1990s TREC news corpora. In technical, statutory, or medical domains, document length variation and repetitive domain nomenclature cause these defaults to degrade recall.

blocks.title: The Long-Document Penalty Flaw
blocks.text: Setting b too high (e.g. 0.85) in legal research harshly penalizes long statutory codes or multi-page court rulings, artificially favoring short procedural notices.

rows: Increase to 1.8 - 2.0 when repeated terms indicate genuine emphasis (e.g. contracts)
Lower to 0.3 - 0.5 for legal statutes where long documents naturally cover more sub-topics
Freeze during evaluation to avoid scoring drift across dataset partitions
Use domain-specific lemmatizers (e.g. Turkish Zemberek / Snowball)

blocks.text: As the count of a query term increases in a document, BM25 increases score asymptotically towards (k1 + 1). Higher k1 values make the curve steeper, rewarding documents with higher repetition of the exact query phrase.

MESA Core leverages SQLite FTS5 with customized column weights and calibrated saturation parameters. Legal article numbers and docket references receive dedicated column multipliers during lexical candidate generation.

Column weights prioritize title and section heading matches.

en.title: Evaluating nDCG, MRR, and Recall@k for agent memory retrieval
en.subtitle: Rigorous ranking metrics for measuring multi-lane hybrid retrieval precision
en.summary: Evaluating agent memory retrieval requires mathematically grounded metrics: Recall@k measures completeness, MRR measures first-hit speed, and nDCG accounts for graded relevance.
en.shortAnswer: Recall@k measures whether the truth was retrieved; MRR measures how early the first hit appeared; nDCG@k measures the quality of the entire top-k ranking.

blocks.text: Teams building agent memory often report a single metric such as 'Recall@10 = 92%'. However, if the correct assertion is consistently ranked at position #9 rather than #1, the downstream generator experiences significant context distraction and token bloat.

blocks.title: Binary Relevance Flaw
blocks.text: Treating all retrieved documents as either 1 (relevant) or 0 (irrelevant) fails in agent workflows where one document contains the primary ruling while two others provide peripheral procedural history.

sections.title: The nDCG discounted cumulative gain equation

blocks.text: Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG) discounts relevance gains logarithmically based on rank position: `DCG@k = Σ (2^{rel_i} - 1) / log_2(i + 1)`. Normalizing by the Ideal DCG (IDCG@k) produces a score in [0.0, 1.0] invariant to list length.

MESA's independent retrieval audit suite tests four distinct retrieval lanes across synthetic and legal golden datasets. The pipeline measures Recall@5, MRR, and nDCG@10 deterministically on every release baseline.

en.title: Embedded graph analytics with Kùzu in memory projections
en.subtitle: High-performance Cypher graph queries without client-server network overhead
en.summary: Kùzu provides an embedded, columnar-storage property graph database optimized for multi-hop graph analytics, making it ideal for derived agent memory projections.
en.shortAnswer: Kùzu embeds directly inside Python and Node processes, executing complex Cypher path traversals over memory triples in microseconds.

blocks.text: Traditional graph databases (Neo4j, TigerGraph) run as standalone JVM or distributed network servers. For agent runtimes, making TCP socket calls and managing external server processes adds 10-30 ms latency per graph query.

blocks.title: The Operational Overhead Hazard
blocks.text: Running dedicated graph database clusters for edge agents or local desktop workflows introduces steep RAM overhead and complex container orchestration requirements.

rows: Embedded in-process C++ library (zero network hop)

sections.title: Columnar property graph storage and factorization

blocks.text: Kùzu uses columnar storage with factorized query execution: intermediate join results are stored as compact factorized tables, preventing the exponential state explosion typical of dense multi-hop graph traversals.

blocks.code:
// Kùzu embedded query invocation in Python
import kuzu
db = kuzu.Database('./kuzu_memory')
conn = kuzu.Connection(db)

blocks.text: MESA Core leverages Kùzu as its specialized graph projection engine. Relational assertions in SQLite are projected into Kùzu nodes and edges, allowing MESA's retrieval router to traverse multi-hop paths instantaneously.

items: Kùzu runs completely in-process alongside SQLite and LanceDB.
Property graph schema mirrors canonical SQLite assertion triples.
Graph projections can be deleted and recomputed deterministically.
Enables lightning-fast 2-hop and 3-hop conflict of interest queries.

en.subtitle: Disk-backed vector search, IVF-PQ indexing, and zero-copy Arrow memory buffers
en.summary: LanceDB uses the columnar Lance format to execute nearest-neighbor vector searches directly against NVMe storage without requiring entire vector indexes to reside in memory.
en.shortAnswer: Lance format decouples vector indexing from RAM limits by using columnar layout, IVF-PQ compression, and Apache Arrow zero-copy access.

sections.title: The RAM explosion in vector databases

blocks.text: Traditional in-memory vector databases (Pinecone, Chroma in-memory) keep entire HNSW graph indexes pinned in system RAM. As an agent's memory scales past millions of chunks, hosting memory becomes prohibitively expensive.

blocks.title: The Memory Exhaustion Crash
blocks.text: Running HNSW graphs in RAM inside agent containers often triggers sudden Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kills when dataset sizes grow unexpectedly during batch ingestion.

rows: Scales to billions of vectors per local disk
Columnar SQL predicates pushed down into disk scan

blocks.text: LanceDB organizes data into columnar chunks where vector arrays and metadata columns are stored contiguously on disk. IVF-PQ partitions vectors into Voronoi cells and compresses float vectors using product quantization codes.

blocks.code:
// LanceDB Python vector search with metadata filter
import lancedb
db = lancedb.connect('./lancedb_memory')
tbl = db.open_table('embeddings')
results = tbl.search(query_vector).where('tenant_id = "corp_a"').limit(10).to_arrow()

blocks.text: MESA Core selects LanceDB as its dedicated dense vector projection layer. Embeddings generated from SQLite assertion passages are projected into Lance tables, ensuring zero-copy sub-millisecond retrieval with minimal RAM consumption.

items: Embeddings are stored in columnar Lance format on local NVMe disk.
Zero-copy Apache Arrow integration eliminates serialization overhead.
Metadata filters execute before nearest-neighbor vector scans.
Projections are ephemeral and deterministically recomputed from SQLite.

en.summary: Enterprise AI memory systems require rigorous Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Row-Level Security (RLS) to ensure editors, viewers, and automated agents operate strictly within permitted security bounds.
en.shortAnswer: RBAC defines what actions users and agents can perform; Row-Level Security enforces which database rows they can view or mutate.

blocks.text: In standard AI chat interfaces, all authenticated users share access to the same retrieval corpus. If a junior contractor queries the system, semantic search can retrieve board meeting minutes or confidential compensation data unless row-level filtering is strictly enforced.

sections.title: Postgres RLS policies and security definer functions

blocks.text: Row-Level Security policies evaluate on every SQL operation. By using `SECURITY DEFINER` functions with fixed `search_path`, permissions are checked against a verified roles table without exposing user elevation vectors.

MESA implements multi-layer authorization across its web CMS and Core engines. The Supabase backend enforces RLS on all eight core tables, while MESA Core applies tenant and workspace isolation in SQLite queries.

items: RLS is enabled on every database table.

en.subtitle: Distinguishing conversational context windows from persistent canonical knowledge
en.summary: AI agents require a strict distinction between ephemeral conversation scratchpads (session state) and validated, long-term factual knowledge (durable memory).
en.shortAnswer: Session state holds temporary conversation turns and scratch reasoning; durable memory holds immutable, verified assertions with long-term validity.

blocks.text: Treating every chat message as permanent long-term memory pollutes the knowledge base with conversational noise, greetings, transient typos, and speculative thoughts that degrade subsequent agent reasoning.

blocks.title: Context Compaction Loss
blocks.text: When an agent's context window fills up, naive compaction algorithms summarize the conversation, often discarding exact citations, character offsets, and source document hashes.

rows: In-memory Redis, process heap, ephemeral KV
Duration of a single user task or conversation
Zero filter: every user message is accepted
Strict: requires schema extraction and evidence validation
Append-only revisions with tamper-evident audit trails
Multi-lane hybrid retrieval (Vector, BM25, Graph, SQL)

blocks.text: At the conclusion of a session, a consolidation worker extracts candidate assertions from the dialogue history. Only assertions that pass schema validation, deduplication checks, and evidence anchoring are admitted into durable memory.

blocks.code:

en.shortAnswer: Average latency hides severe tail-latency spikes. Systems must benchmark p95 and p99 response times across concurrent retrieval lanes.

blocks.text: Reporting mean latency (e.g. 'Average query latency is 15 ms') conceals catastrophic tail latencies where 5% of queries hang for 500 ms due to unindexed graph traversals or thread pool exhaustion.

blocks.title: Tail Latency Contagion
blocks.text: In multi-lane architectures where four lanes run concurrently, the slowest lane dictates the overall response time: overall latency equals max(lane_1, lane_2, lane_3, lane_4).

Hybrid retrieval dispatches concurrent queries using non-blocking asynchronous runtimes. A strict per-lane timeout budget prevents a runaway graph traversal from holding up the overall search pipeline.

MESA's automated benchmark suites measure p50, p95, and p99 latencies on every build. Because SQLite, LanceDB, and Kùzu all execute in-process without network hops, MESA achieves sub-15ms p99 end-to-end multi-lane retrieval.

items: Zero network socket hops eliminate inter-process latency overhead.
Asynchronous query dispatch executes all four lanes concurrently.
Per-lane timeout guards ensure predictable tail latencies.
CI performance regression gates block commits that increase p99 latency.

en.shortAnswer: Statute invalidation uses provenance dependency graphs to retract obsolete legal interpretations the moment legislation changes.

blocks.text: Legal language models trained on static corpora frequently cite repealed articles or overturned judicial precedents as if they remain current positive law, exposing practitioners to grave professional liability.

blocks.title: The Anachronistic Precedent Hazard
blocks.text: A Supreme Court decision from 2018 may have correctly interpreted Article 40 under prior law, but subsequent 2022 legislative reform may have rendered that precedent legally void.

MESA Law maps official Turkish legislative gazettes and judicial decisions to immutable byte records. Its provenance engine tracks temporal validity windows, ensuring no agent ever cites repealed statutory provisions.

blocks.text: Standard RAG breaks documents into independent chunks (e.g. 500 tokens). When an answer requires combining Fact 1 from Document A with Fact 2 from Document B and Fact 3 from Document C, flat vector search fails because no single chunk satisfies the query.

blocks.text: Dense vector similarity cannot verify multi-step transitive logic: knowing A is related to B, and B is related to C, does not mathematically guarantee that A and C share a specific contractual obligation.
